title: CEO Interview with Sander den Hoedt of Delmic - Semiwiki
gist: Delmic, a 2011 TU Delft/AMOLF spin-out with 220+ customers in 30+ countries, sells automated cathodoluminescence (CL) electron-microscopy workflows (SPARC, FLASH) that let compound-semiconductor R&D teams (GaN, SiC, µLEDs, quantum emitters) get yield-defect data back in hours instead of weeks, differentiating by pairing best-in-class third-party SEM columns with full workflow automation rather than building a proprietary electron column.

insights.claim: Delmic was founded in 2011 as a spin-out of TU Delft and AMOLF after a TU Delft professor suggested combining light and electron microscopy; founder Sander den Hoedt and co-founder Andries Effting took the resulting patent out of the university to start the company.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A university-patent-to-startup origin with 15 years of operating history suggests durable core IP (combined light/electron microscopy) rather than a recent opportunistic pivot into semiconductor characterization.

insights.claim: Den Hoedt's core conviction is that almost every process that matters plays out at the nanoscale, yet the instruments that look at that scale are still operated by hand, which he compares to 'a Ferrari permanently stuck in traffic'; Delmic's purpose is framed as removing that traffic.
insights.speaker: Sander den Hoedt
insights.so_what: This 'high-resolution instrument, manual bottleneck' framing is the core investment thesis for automation vendors in metrology/characterization — the addressable value is in workflow automation, not raw instrument resolution, which is already commoditized.
insights.quote: A Ferrari permanently stuck in traffic.

insights.claim: Delmic is headquartered in Delft with presence in Japan and the United States, and today more than 220 research institutes and companies in over 30 countries use its technology.
insights.speaker: Sander den Hoedt
insights.so_what: 220+ customers across 30+ countries indicates meaningful global installed-base scale for a specialized deep-tech instrumentation vendor, useful for benchmarking market penetration in a niche characterization-tools category.

themes.theme: Cathodoluminescence as the semiconductor R&D wedge

insights.claim: Delmic's SPARC platform is described as the leading tool for characterizing compound semiconductors and related materials — including GaN, SiC, µLED and quantum emitters — at the nanoscale, with 100+ systems installed globally; the newer FLASH platform extends this into industrial R&D.
insights.speaker: Sander den Hoedt
insights.so_what: 100+ installed SPARC systems in compound-semiconductor materials positions Delmic as an incumbent supplier just as GaN/SiC power electronics demand accelerates (EVs, AI datacenter power delivery), making it a potential acquisition target or bellwether for compound-semi capex.
insights.locator: "Tell us about your company" section, SPARC/FLASH description

insights.claim: Den Hoedt argues the microscope itself is no longer the resolution limit for many applications; the manual work around it (sample loading, acquisition, choosing where to measure) is now the bottleneck, since these steps still depend on expert operators.
insights.speaker: Sander den Hoedt
insights.so_what: If resolution is solved and operator time is the constraint, the addressable market shifts from hardware upgrades to software/automation upsells on existing installed SEM base — a higher-margin, stickier revenue model.

insights.claim: In compound semiconductors, yield-limiting defects are often invisible to optical inspection because they are too deep or too small, leaving today's feedback loop either incomplete (optical inspection) or very slow (electron microscopy); Delmic automates measurement so data returns in hours instead of weeks.
insights.speaker: Sander den Hoedt
insights.so_what: Cutting defect feedback loops from weeks to hours directly compresses process-development iteration cycles for GaN/SiC fabs, a measurable yield-ramp accelerant that customers can quantify in cost-per-wafer terms.
insights.locator: "What problems are you solving?" section, feedback-loop discussion

insights.claim: As GaN and SiC wafers scale to 200 mm and 300 mm and new compound-semiconductor fabs come online, competitive pressure increases because slow yield feedback loops become more costly when competitors can iterate faster.
insights.speaker: Sander den Hoedt
insights.so_what: The 200mm/300mm GaN/SiC wafer transition is a concrete industry milestone that should expand demand for fast nanoscale characterization tools like Delmic's, signaling a tailwind tied to a specific, trackable capacity-expansion trend.
insights.locator: "What keeps your customers up at night?" section

insights.claim: Beneath the yield problem, researchers across every segment Delmic serves often draw conclusions from very limited measurements simply because measuring takes too long, creating a broader 'data-confidence problem' about whether observed results are the rule or a coincidence.
insights.speaker: Sander den Hoedt
insights.so_what: The 'data-confidence problem' framework — statistical robustness limited by measurement throughput, not just measurement quality — is a generalizable lens for evaluating any metrology/characterization vendor's true value proposition versus raw instrument specs.
insights.locator: "What keeps your customers up at night?" section, closing paragraph

insights.claim: Den Hoedt says competitors in cathodoluminescence fall into two camps: providers of hardware-agnostic add-on CL detectors that leave the workflow dependent on operator expertise with little automation, or providers who pursue integrated CL-SEM with their own proprietary electron column that is widely regarded as underperforming on electron-optical quality; Delmic instead pairs best-in-class third-party electron columns with full integration and automation.
insights.speaker: Sander den Hoedt
insights.so_what: Deliberately not building a proprietary electron column (unlike rivals) is a capital-efficient differentiation strategy — Delmic avoids competing on core SEM hardware R&D and instead wins on integration/software, a moat worth monitoring against OEM electron-microscope makers entering CL directly.
insights.locator: "What does the competitive landscape look like" section

insights.claim: Delmic differentiates on four dimensions: broad modality coverage (six CL imaging modes including time-resolved measurement and polarimetry), compatibility with high-quality commercial SEMs rather than a proprietary column, one of the largest installed bases and applications maps in the field, and increasing automation of the complete measurement workflow.
insights.speaker: Sander den Hoedt
insights.so_what: A four-pillar differentiation framework (modality breadth, hardware neutrality, installed-base scale, automation) gives a concrete scorecard for assessing whether new entrants (e.g., electron-microscope OEMs) could disrupt Delmic's position.
insights.locator: "What does the competitive landscape look like" section, closing summary

insights.claim: Delmic's next-generation SPARC 3.0 platform, launching at IMC21, adds automation out of the box such as whole-wafer mapping and automatic selection of measurement locations; combined with its ODEMIS control software, the instrument now drives the beam, stage and detector autonomously and delivers analysis-ready data.
insights.speaker: Sander den Hoedt
insights.so_what: SPARC 3.0's autonomous whole-wafer mapping is a concrete near-term product catalyst (launching at IMC21 in Liverpool) that could accelerate adoption among compound-semiconductor fabs seeking faster, less labor-intensive yield characterization.
insights.locator: "What new features / technology are you working on?" section

insights.claim: Delmic is also developing next generations of its FLASH platform for compound-semiconductor R&D and working on AI-assisted analysis intended to act as a validated gateway to existing community and commercial analysis models rather than building proprietary analysis models from scratch.
insights.speaker: Sander den Hoedt
insights.so_what: Choosing to be a validated gateway to third-party AI analysis models (rather than reinventing them) is a capital-light AI integration strategy, reducing R&D risk while still capturing an AI-enabled feature set customers increasingly expect.
insights.locator: "What new features / technology are you working on?" section, closing sentence

insights.claim: Entry-level CL detectors typically have a shorter sales cycle and are often sold through OEM or distributor partners, while flagship platforms such as FLASH involve a longer, consultative sales process sold directly in Europe and North America, with distributor support across Asia-Pacific.
insights.speaker: Sander den Hoedt
insights.so_what: A tiered go-to-market (fast OEM-channel entry products vs. long-cycle direct-sold flagship platforms) suggests Delmic's revenue mix likely combines a shorter-cycle volume base with a higher-value, longer-cycle enterprise tail — relevant for forecasting revenue lumpiness.
